text: Neptune and Triton is an early marble sculpture created by the Italian artist Gian Lorenzo Bernini, executed around 1622–1623 and standing 182.2 cm (71.7 in) tall. It was originally commissioned by Cardinal Alessandro Damascenti-Peretti Montalto in 1620 and completed from March 1622 to February 1623 as a fountain to decorate the pond in the garden of his Villa Peretti Montalto on the Viminal Hill in Rome. The sculpture was placed in the pre-existing oval pool, the Peschiera or Peschierone, designed by Domenico Fontana between 1579 and 1581. The work was initially referred to as "Neptune and Glaucus" in Filippo Baldinucci's biography of Bernini, but appears as "Nettvno, e Tritone" in Domenico de' Rossi's engraving from 1704 and was later corrected to "Neptune and Triton" based on Joshua Reynolds' notes. In 1786, the Englishman Thomas Jenkins purchased it, and later that same year, Joshua Reynolds acquired it. After Reynolds' death in 1792, it was sold to Charles Anderson-Pelham, 1st Baron Yarborough, who kept it in the garden of his home, Walpole House, in Chelsea, London. His descendants moved it in 1906 to Brocklesby Hall in Lincolnshire. The Victoria and Albert Museum in London bought the sculpture in 1950, although it had previously been exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1938. The scene draws loose allusions to Neptune and Triton aiding Trojan ships as described in Virgil's Aeneid and Ovid's Metamorphoses. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Neptune commands Triton to blow his shell to calm the waves, while in Virgil's Aeneid, Neptune calms the waves and later, with the nereid Cymothoe and Triton, dislodges Aeneas's ships using his trident. However, neither passage precisely matches the sculpture, and Bernini appears to have combined elements from various sources. The composition features Neptune standing astride over Triton, who is in a crouching position, both mounted on a large half-shell serving as socle. Neptune aims his trident seawards, while Triton blows his conch, designed to spurt water, making the sculpture functional as a fountain. Neptune's posture and the filling of the reverse-V-shaped negative space by Triton represent radical departures in Bernini's work, marking his first piece where the silhouette is broken and demonstrating "full Baroque freedom" according to Rudolf Wittkower, though Wittkower noted Bernini had not yet achieved the dynamism seen in later works like David and Pluto. Neptune is depicted as a mature, bearded, muscular figure of male authority, twisting his torso as if about to thrust his trident downward, wearing a cloak and being otherwise naked; his touseled hair and beard suggest storminess. Wittkower interpreted Neptune's angry expression as calming the waves with his trident, while John Pope-Hennessy noted the absence of the nereid in the Virgilian scene and suggested Ovid as a basis, though the Ovid passage fails to mention the trident. Collier pointed out the inconsistency of Neptune wearing a wrathful expression while calming the sea and proposed an Ovid passage where Neptune is in wrath, but this also lacks mention of the trident. Collier also suggested that if Virgil was the source, Neptune might be using the trident to dislodge ships from rocks, but the absence of any ships in the sculpture makes this implausible. Notably, the ends of Neptune's drapery resemble dolphin heads, possibly paying homage to Ovid's references to Neptune and dolphins in the Metamorphoses and the theme of transformation, or reflecting a light-hearted Hellenistic Rococo touch as perceived by Barrow. Triton, Neptune's son, is positioned below Neptune's legs, thrusting forward to blow the conch, appearing as a teenage boy with defined musculature; he grasps Neptune's leg and ducks his left shoulder between Neptune's thighs. Bernini's Triton is double-tailed, a feature also seen in his later Triton Fountain in Rome. The naturalism of the figures aims to evoke an immediate emotional response: Neptune's furrowed brow conveys fierce strength and divine power, while Triton appears submissive and anxious, reflecting human emotion and obedience. Bernini's work allows viewers to "see" the gods in motion, marking his first sculpture where the silhouette is broken, the climax of a transitory action is presented, and the action extends beyond physical limits. The sculpture's dramatic body positions and subtle naturalism are intended to make myths feel real and demand viewer belief in their truth.
